source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
One campus in Durham holds 80 percent of North Carolina's disclosed data center capacity, and 14 of the state's 19 mapped facilities publish no capacity at all.

CyrusOne's DUR1 and DUR2 list 40 MW of IT capacity across 420,000 square feet of technical space. That is the largest published figure in North Carolina among the five facilities that disclose megawatts. The 80 percent share is a share of what has been published, not of what exists. With 14 of 19 facilities silent, the state's actual inventory is unknown and almost certainly larger than the disclosed total.

For AI, megawatts of IT capacity are the closest public proxy for how much compute a site can host. But 40 MW is a nameplate number. The specifications do not state the power infrastructure serving the site, the PUE, the grid operator for Durham, or any power purchase agreements. Without those, nothing here indicates whether the capacity can run continuously, or at what utilization the local grid would permit. The implied counts of roughly 400 racks and 1,280 accelerators are arithmetic on assumed densities, not operator disclosures, and the operator publishes no breakdown by workload or tenant class.

The record also carries no certifications and no announced expansion, which the suitability score flags as a missing input. A single campus page cannot describe a state's position on the grid, and this one does not try to. What it establishes is narrower and still useful: one operator has disclosed more capacity in North Carolina than every other disclosing operator combined, while most of the state's mapped footprint remains unquantified.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
